prompt: After every row of the copy was updated once and then vacuumed, the table was 130 MB instead of 66 MB. What is in the extra 64 MB?
hint: VACUUM had already run.

choices.text: Dead versions waiting for the next VACUUM
choices.why: VACUUM had run; pgstattuple later counted 0 dead tuples.

choices.text: A second copy of the indexes, which VACUUM keeps for rollback
choices.why: The indexes are measured separately, at 75 MB; the table's own file holds no index.

choices.text: Free space
choices.why: Right. The old versions were freed and the room stayed inside the file.

choices.text: Write-ahead log for the UPDATE
choices.why: WAL lives in pg_wal, not in the table's file.

prompt: Deleting the top 100,000 ids and vacuuming left the copy at 130 MB; deleting the next 100,000 took it to 117 MB. Why the difference?
hint: VACUUM truncates only a tail big enough.

choices.text: The first DELETE had not committed yet
choices.why: psql commits each statement by itself; the deleted rows were dead before the VACUUM.

choices.text: The second VACUUM ran as VACUUM FULL
choices.why: Both were plain VACUUM; a FULL would have taken the table to about 52 MB.

choices.text: Only the second delete reached rows stored at the start of the file
choices.why: Only empty pages at the end of the file are cut; the start of the file is never returned by a plain VACUUM.

choices.text: The first tail was under 1,000 pages and under a sixteenth of the table
choices.why: Right. Truncating needs a brief exclusive lock, and VACUUM only takes it for a tail past one of those limits.

prompt: Which of these is NOT a cost of a table that is half free space?
hint: Think of what reads the whole file, and what reads only rows.

choices.text: Sequential scans read the empty space too
choices.why: They do: a sequential scan reads every page.

choices.text: Backups copy it
choices.why: A file-level backup copies the file, empty space included.

choices.text: The disk holds it and the operating system cannot use it
choices.why: That is exactly what bloat costs a disk.

choices.text: Wrong query results
choices.why: Right. Free space holds no rows, so bloat never changes an answer; it only costs reading and storage.

prompt: What `free_percent` did `pgstattuple` report for the bloated copy? Answer to the nearest whole number.
hint: A little more than half.

prompt: `pgstattuple_approx` answered with `scanned_percent` 0 and a row count of 902,407 for a table holding 800,000. Why was the count off?
hint: It read no pages. Where did the number come from?

choices.text: From statistics taken before the last DELETE
choices.why: Right. The row count comes from the planner's estimate, which was older than the delete.

choices.text: It counts dead tuples as live
choices.why: There were no dead tuples; VACUUM had run.

choices.text: Its sampling of a few random pages happened to land on fuller ones
choices.why: It scanned 0% of the table; there was no sample at all.

choices.text: pg_repack had not yet run
choices.why: pg_repack changes the file, not how an estimate is made.

prompt: A monitoring tool's estimate reports 12% bloat on a table that was bulk-loaded last night and never updated. What is the most likely reading?
hint: Remember the `orders` line.

choices.text: The load left dead versions behind
choices.why: A load of inserts leaves live rows, not dead ones.

choices.text: The table needs VACUUM FULL tonight
choices.why: Nothing has been measured yet; rebuilding on an estimate's word buys an exclusive lock for nothing.

choices.text: The estimate's own error; measure with pgstattuple before acting
choices.why: Right. On orders, which has no bloat, the same arithmetic showed about a tenth of the table as wasted.

choices.text: The fill factor of the table was lowered during the load
choices.why: Nothing in the scenario changed a fill factor; the estimate's padding error explains the number by itself.

prompt: Why run `pgstattuple` on a 500 GB table at a quiet hour?
hint: How did it get an exact answer?

choices.text: It locks the table against writes
choices.why: It only reads, with the lock any SELECT takes.

choices.text: It rewrites the table to count it
choices.why: That is VACUUM FULL. pgstattuple writes nothing.

choices.text: It reads every page through shared buffers
choices.why: Right. Exact means a full scan, and 500 GB of reading competes with the application.

choices.text: It needs the server restarted to load
choices.why: CREATE EXTENSION pgstattuple worked without a restart.

prompt: Which `pgstatindex` column is the number to act on for index bloat?
hint: How full are the leaves?

choices.text: leaf_fragmentation
choices.why: orders_customer_id is near 50 with no bloat at all; fragmentation is a detail.

choices.text: tree_level
choices.why: Depth grows with size slowly and says little about wasted space.

choices.text: root_block_no
choices.why: That is where the root page sits, not how full anything is.

choices.text: avg_leaf_density
choices.why: Right. The copy's primary key at 45 against 90 for the original is the bloat.

prompt: `orders_created_at` sits at 78% leaf density although `orders` has never been updated. What does that tell you?
hint: How did its keys arrive?

choices.text: It is bloated and should be reindexed
choices.why: Nothing dead is in it; out-of-order inserts split leaves and they settle below 90.

choices.text: Its fill factor was set to 78
choices.why: Nobody set one; the default for a B-tree is 90.

choices.text: 90% is the wrong yardstick here
choices.why: Right. Compare an index with the same index unbloated, not with a fixed number.

choices.text: pgstatindex cannot read timestamp columns
choices.why: It reads any B-tree; the column type is irrelevant.

prompt: An `UPDATE` changes only `status`, which no index covers, on a table whose pages have plenty of free room. What happens to the table's indexes?
hint: HOT.

choices.text: Nothing: the update is HOT
choices.why: Right. The new version stays on the same page and no index is touched, which is what a lower table fillfactor buys room for.

choices.text: Every index gets a new entry
choices.why: That is the non-HOT case: no room on the page, or an indexed column changed.

choices.text: Only the primary key gets a new entry
choices.why: A non-HOT update touches every index, and a HOT one touches none.

choices.text: The indexes are rebuilt at the next VACUUM
choices.why: VACUUM removes dead entries; it never rebuilds an index.

prompt: While `VACUUM FULL orders_copy` ran, a plain `SELECT count(*)` on the copy waited. Which lock was it waiting for?
hint: Read the granted column.

choices.text: AccessExclusiveLock
choices.why: That is the one VACUUM FULL held, granted.

choices.text: ShareLock
choices.why: Those rows belonged to the index builds inside the rebuild.

choices.text: AccessShareLock
choices.why: Right: the weakest lock there is, and it still conflicts with the AccessExclusiveLock VACUUM FULL holds.

choices.text: A row lock on the first row
choices.why: A count takes no row locks; it waited at the table.

prompt: Match each fact to the tool it belongs to.
hint: One is built in, one is installed.

pairs.left: Holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE from start to finish
Needs a primary key or a unique not-null index
Frees space for reuse without returning it

prompt: A disk is 95% full, and most of it is one bloated table. Why might `VACUUM FULL` fail to fix it?
hint: When is the old file removed?

choices.text: It refuses tables over a size limit
choices.why: There is no such limit.

choices.text: It needs the WAL to hold the whole table first, so it fills pg_wal on a separate disk
choices.why: The problem is on this disk: the old and new files coexist until the swap.

choices.text: The new file is written before the old one goes
choices.why: Right. It needs room for the compact copy and its indexes while the bloated ones still exist; pg_repack has the same need.

choices.text: It needs the server stopped
choices.why: It ran on a running server; it only locks the one table.

prompt: You start `pg_repack` on a busy table at noon. A report has held a transaction on that table since 11:00. What happens at the swap?
hint: The swap needs a brief exclusive lock.

choices.text: The swap goes through, since pg_repack only needs AccessShareLock
choices.why: It holds AccessShareLock while copying; the swap still needs the exclusive lock for a moment.

choices.text: It finishes the swap at once and the report reads the new file
choices.why: An exclusive lock cannot be granted while the report holds the table.

choices.text: It waits, queries queue behind it, and after 60 s it cancels the report
choices.why: Right, by default. --no-kill-backend makes it give up instead.

choices.text: It falls back to VACUUM FULL
choices.why: pg_repack has no such fallback.

prompt: Put pg_repack's work in order.
hint: Exclusive at both ends, shared in the middle.
items: A brief exclusive lock to set up the trigger
Copy the rows into a new table while the trigger records changes
Build the indexes on the new table
A brief exclusive lock to swap the files
trap: The changes are replayed before the swap, so nothing written during the copy is lost.

prompt: After a rebuild to 52 MB, three rounds of updating a fifth of the rows left the copy at 63 MB, 63 MB and 63 MB. What is 63 MB?
hint: The second and third rounds did not grow it.

choices.text: Its working size
choices.why: Right. Rebuilding back to 52 MB would only last until the next round of updates.

choices.text: Bloat that the next rebuild should remove for good
choices.why: Space reused round after round is the healthy shape, not bloat to remove.

choices.text: A limit autovacuum enforces
choices.why: Nothing caps the size; reuse of freed space kept it steady.

choices.text: The size of the indexes
choices.why: The indexes were measured beside it, at 56 to 57 MB.

prompt: Which of these justify rebuilding a bloated table? Choose all that apply.
hint: Will the traffic ever use the space?

choices.text: A one-off backfill doubled it
choices.why: Yes. The space will not be reused at the rate it was made.

choices.text: The disk is running out now
choices.why: Yes, if there is room for the new copy while it is built.

choices.text: Its free percentage has been steady for months
choices.why: Steady free space is being reused; a rebuild would grow back.

choices.text: It grew back to the same size within days of the last rebuild
choices.why: That is its working size telling you so.

choices.text: Its sequential scans read mostly empty pages
choices.why: Yes, when pgstattuple confirms it.

prompt: To leave a tenth of each page empty so updates can stay on the same page, set the table's ___ to 90.
hint: A storage parameter set with ALTER TABLE ... SET.

prompt: A 400 GB `events` table is 60% free space according to pgstattuple, after a purge of two years of old rows. The application inserts 1 GB a day. What is the right move?
hint: How long would the traffic take to reuse 240 GB?

choices.text: Leave it: the inserts will reuse the space
choices.why: At 1 GB a day, 240 GB takes most of a year. This is the one-off case.

choices.text: VACUUM it, which returns the free space
choices.why: A plain VACUUM returns only an empty tail; the free space is spread through the file.

choices.text: VACUUM FULL it during business hours
choices.why: That blocks every query on events for as long as copying 160 GB takes.

choices.text: pg_repack it, with room for the 160 GB copy
choices.why: Right. A purge is a one-off, and pg_repack keeps the table usable while the live 160 GB are copied.

prompt: After `pg_repack` the copy's indexes were 31 MB; one round of updating a fifth of the rows took them to 56 MB, while the table grew only from 52 MB to 63 MB. Why did the indexes grow so much more?
hint: Freshly built leaves are 90% full.

choices.text: pg_repack builds indexes without a fill factor
choices.why: They were built at the default 90%, like VACUUM FULL's.

choices.text: The trigger pg_repack left behind writes extra index entries
choices.why: The trigger is removed at the swap; nothing of pg_repack's stays on the table.

choices.text: Non-HOT updates added entries to full leaves, which split
choices.why: Right. Each new version needed an entry in every index, and a full leaf splits into two half-full pages.

choices.text: VACUUM did not run on the indexes
choices.why: VACUUM ran each round; the size stayed near 56 MB in the next two rounds.

prompt: Lesson 14 left a table bloated by a session idle in transaction for a day. You run `pg_repack` before ending that session. What do you get?
hint: Which versions does the copy have to keep?

choices.text: A wait at the swap, and no lasting fix
choices.why: Right. End the session first: as long as it holds the horizon, dead versions pile up again whatever is rebuilt.

choices.text: A compact table, since pg_repack ignores snapshots
choices.why: It does not ignore them; and the session holds the table, so the swap cannot even get its lock.

choices.text: An error that the table has no primary key
choices.why: Nothing in the scenario removes the key; the held snapshot is the problem.

choices.text: The idle session is ended automatically by pg_repack before the copy starts
choices.why: pg_repack cancels conflicting queries only at the lock waits, after a timeout.

prompt: While `pg_repack` copied the rows, which lock did it hold on `orders_copy`?
hint: The UPDATE from another terminal went straight through.

choices.text: AccessExclusiveLock for the whole copy, released only at the end
choices.why: That is VACUUM FULL's way. pg_repack takes the exclusive lock only for a moment at each end.

choices.text: No lock at all
choices.why: pg_locks showed AccessShareLock held by its sessions.

choices.text: AccessShareLock, as a SELECT does
choices.why: Right, plus an SIReadLock from copying at SERIALIZABLE. Neither blocks reads or writes.

choices.text: ShareLock, which allows reads and blocks writes
choices.why: A ShareLock would have made the UPDATE wait; it took a few milliseconds.

prompt: A nightly job deletes the oldest 1% of `events` rows, and the application inserts about as many new rows each day. Will the table's file keep growing?
hint: Where do the new rows go once VACUUM has run?

choices.text: Yes, by 1% a day, since VACUUM returns nothing
choices.why: VACUUM returns nothing to the operating system, but the freed room is reused by the next inserts.

choices.text: No, because DELETE shrinks the file immediately
choices.why: A DELETE only marks versions dead; the file stays as it was.

choices.text: No, once vacuumed the freed space takes the new rows
choices.why: Right. The free space map sends inserts into the room the deletes left, and the size settles.

choices.text: Yes, unless the job also runs VACUUM FULL every night
choices.why: A nightly VACUUM FULL would lock the table every night for nothing; plain VACUUM and reuse keep the size steady.
